Finnish Economy Reels as Euro Plunge Sparks Crisis; Metso Oyj Cuts Output

HELSINKI – Finland faces mounting economic turmoil as the euro’s sudden collapse against major currencies this month sends shockwaves through the nation’s financial system, threatening jobs and investment across key sectors.

The euro, Finland’s currency since 1999, fell to record lows against the US dollar and Swedish krona last week after a volatile period marked by increasing investor anxiety over European sovereign debt. The Finnish central bank confirmed on Wednesday that the euro’s value against the dollar had dropped by 23 percent since early May, fueling immediate concerns about import costs, inflation, and financial stability.

Prime Minister Sanna Lehto addressed the nation on Tuesday evening, warning that the “unprecedented volatility in the currency markets has placed extraordinary pressure on Finland’s economy. The government is working closely with European partners and the Bank of Finland to stabilize the situation.”

Across industries, companies are feeling the strain. Metso Oyj, a major supplier of technology and services for the process industries, announced temporary production cutbacks at its Tampere and Jyväskylä facilities as a result of disrupted supply chains and soaring expenses for imported components. In a statement, Metso Oyj’s Chief Operating Officer, Ari Nieminen, said, “We are closely monitoring the situation and adjusting our operations to protect both our employees and our long-term competitiveness. The sharp increase in import costs has forced us to reconsider our production schedules.”

The Confederation of Finnish Industries estimated on Wednesday that manufacturing output nationwide could fall by as much as 7 percent this quarter if currency instability persists. “We are seeing cost pressures that are unprecedented in recent memory, and many firms face serious liquidity challenges,” said chief economist Katja Virtanen.

For ordinary Finns, the crisis is most visible at the grocery store and petrol station. The National Consumer Union reported that food prices have risen by an average of 12 percent since the start of June, while fuel costs have surged by nearly 20 percent. “If this continues, we’ll see families making tough choices about what they can afford,” warned union chair Jussi Peltonen.

The government has convened emergency talks with labour leaders and industry groups to discuss possible support measures, but opposition politicians have called for more decisive intervention, including temporary price controls on essential goods.

With the euro still tumbling and uncertainty clouding Finland’s economic outlook, analysts warn the nation faces a pivotal summer. “We’re only at the beginning of this crisis,” said Nordmark Bank strategist Elina Miettinen. “How Finland adapts in the coming weeks will shape our recovery for years to come.”
